newsitem.title: FRANCE: New French education minister Allegre is scientist.
newsitem.headline: New French education minister Allegre is scientist.

text.p: Claude Allegre, France's new minister of education, research and technology, is best known abroad for his knowledge of minerals. But his path to the cabinet may have been helped by his tennis game.

Allegre, 60, is a longtime tennis partner to Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin. He has also been one of his closest advisers on issues ranging from science and education policy to European integration.
Allegre, a workaholic outspoken at times to the point of being rude, has been close to the newly-appointed Socialist prime minister for some four decades and a key adviser since at least the 1980s.
Their friendship dates back to their student days when they both worked against France's war on Algerian independence fighters as part of a campaign led by the UNEF students' union.
Allegre has a worldwide reputation as a scientist in the relatively obscure field of earth sciences, dealing primarily with minerals and mining.

He has published numerous articles in international science journals and was chairman until recently of France's Office of Geological and Mining Research (BRGM), an applied research and mining organisation.

He was sacked as BRGM chairman by outgoing industry minister Franck Borotra (RPR) in April after opposing a plan to group BRGM's mining assets with other national mining properties. He remains a professor at the University of Paris' Jussieu campus.

Jospin first named Allegre president of the Socialist party's group of experts in 1985, when he became leader of the Socialist Party. Three years later, Jospin was named education minister and made him his special adviser.
He was one of Jospin's top advisers during the 1995 presidential campaign, when Jospin came much closer than expected to defeating Gaullist Jacques Chirac.
When Jospin returned to the Socialist Party following the 1995 campaign, Allegre turned more to his duties at the BRGM but resumed advising Jospin in the parliamentary election campaign.
Allegre is a strong supporter of European monetary union but opposes early eastward expansion of the European Union.

"We must refuse any attempt at enlargement, whatever one may think about this or that country," he wrote recently. "One must finish the house's foundation before building more floors. Before any expansion, we need to make the current EU stronger."
Allegre urged a reaffirmation across the EU of the importance of the public sector and the elimination of all EU requirements opening up national industries to competition.
